**How to Make Traditional Korean Sikhye (Rice‑Sweetened Drink)** > *Sikhye* (식혜) is a mildly sweet, slightly alcoholic rice drink made from glutinous rice grains soaked overnight and then boiled with malt powder. It’s usually served chilled during holidays or after meals. Below you’ll find a classic recipe plus some handy tips if you’d like to tweak flavors or textures. --- ### Ingredients | Item | Amount | |------|--------| | Glutinous (sticky) short‑grain rice | **1 cup** (≈200 g) – rinsed until water runs clear | | Malt powder (maltodextrin) | **2–3 tbsp** (adjust sweetness & body) | | Water | **5 cups** (~1200 ml) + extra for soaking | | Optional flavorings | • Sweet potato starch or tapioca flour (for thicker mouthfeel)
• A pinch of salt
• Honey/white sugar (to taste) | *(If you’re making “sweet” sikhye, add honey/sugar at the end; for “plain,” skip.)* --- ### Equipment Needed - Large bowl or pot for soaking - Medium saucepan for boiling - Fine strainer or cheesecloth - Measuring spoons / kitchen scale - Small ladle or spoon for serving --- ### Step‑by‑Step Instructions #### 1️⃣ Prepare the Rice 1. Rinse the sticky rice under cold running water until the water stays relatively clear. 2. Drain thoroughly and place into a clean bowl. Add enough fresh water so the rice sits about an inch below the surface—roughly **½ cup** per cup of dry rice. 3. Cover tightly and let soak **overnight (8–12 h)** at room temperature. If you’re pressed for time, a quick soak works too: bring to boil, simmer 15 min, cool, cover, and refrigerate for ~4 hrs. #### 2️⃣ Boil the Mixture 1. After soaking, drain the excess water while keeping the rice intact. 2. Transfer the soaked rice back into your saucepan. Pour in **5 cups** of fresh water (the same amount you originally added). 3. Bring to a gentle boil over high heat. Once bubbling, reduce to low and let simmer uncovered for **30–45 minutes**, stirring occasionally. You’ll see small translucent pearls forming around the rice grains—that’s the hallmark of good sikhye! #### 3️⃣ Strain & Cool 1. Remove from heat and strain through a fine mesh sieve lined with cheesecloth or a nut milk bag. Press gently to extract all liquid. 2. Let the strained liquid sit at room temp for another **20 minutes** to allow sediment to settle. Then pour off the top layer into a separate container, leaving behind the thick, milky residue (this will become part of the next batch). #### 4️⃣ Flavor & Sweeten 1. Dissolve the malt powder in a little warm water first (about ¼ cup) to avoid clumps. Stir this solution into the cooled liquid. 2. Taste! If you prefer sweeter sikhye, stir in honey or white sugar gradually until you reach the desired level. - *Tip:* Adding a pinch of salt balances the sweetness and enhances aroma. 3. Optionally mix in a tablespoon of sweet potato starch dissolved in a splash of water to thicken the texture further. #### 5️⃣ Chill & Serve 1. Refrigerate the finished sikhye for at least **2 hours** before serving. 2. When ready, pour into glasses, garnish with a few whole rice grains left in the bottom of the pan, and enjoy immediately. - *Serving suggestion:* Place a handful of leftover rice grains in each glass—they float beautifully and look festive. --- ### Variations & Tips | Variation | How to Do It | Why Try It? | |-----------|--------------|-------------| | **Mild Alcoholic Version** | Keep the residual rice‑starch mixture (step 3) aside. Reheat it slowly with a bit of malt powder and let ferment naturally for 24 hours at room temp. Mix a portion back into the main brew. | Adds subtle depth and complexity. | | **Tapioca‑Starch Thickening** | Replace sweet potato starch with equal amounts of tapioca flour mixed with a dash of hot water. | Gives silky mouthfeel similar to traditional sikhye. | | **Fruit Infusion** | Drop dried persimmon slices or dried apricot pieces into step 2 when boiling. | Enhances natural sweetness and adds aromatic nuance. | | **Low‑Sugar Alternative** | Use only malt powder and omit additional sugars/honey. | Keeps calorie count lower while still delivering authentic flavor. | --- ### Quick FAQ - **Can I use regular rice instead of sticky rice?** Sticky rice gives the characteristic pearl formation. Regular rice yields a thinner drink; try mixing half sticky, half regular for balance. - **What does the “pearl” mean?** Those tiny translucent spheres are formed from gelatinized starch released by the sticky rice. They’re essential for proper texture. - **Is there a risk of mold?** As long as you keep everything covered and refrigerated promptly, mold won’t develop. However, always discard any cloudy or foul‑smelling batches. Enjoy crafting your own homemade sikhye—a delightful treat that pairs wonderfully with savory dishes or simply as a refreshing summer cooler!
